title: Most important investment incentive
primary_topics: Trustworthiness-as-most-important-investment-incentive column May 26, 2013 -- third of automated-elections quadrilogy + first JFC-pained-letter article (later sequel A457 June 9)

PNoy 'thumbed down proposals to change economic provisions of our Constitution' -- officials should turn to other ways of attracting long-term FDIs; FDIs 'spur inclusive growth, alleviate poverty and create jobs'; come in trickles to PH but 'poured massively on neighboring countries like Malaysia, Thailand, Singapore and Indonesia'

Trustworthiness thesis: 'most important incentive to bring them in -- trustworthiness of our government -- has been neglected; Past regimes are not famous for honoring their word; Can the present administration be trusted? Is it sensitive and responsive to investors' cry for fairness, honesty and transparency?'

JFC pained-letter test: 'Joint Foreign Chambers (JFC) lamenting failure of government to fulfill its commitments... lament cannot be ignored because JFC represents largest existing FDIs in Philippines'

Large-foreign-investors choice-framework: 'safe' money + 'easy or difficult' to do business + 'how much they would earn for the risks they take'; countries compete by offering 'tax- and duty-free importation of capital equipment'; consumer-trade parallel -- 'people choose and buy cars of specific brand because they trust its engineering, beauty, after-sale service and used-car prices'

Pained-letter on 1990s power-outage FDI bait: government promised many fiscal incentives + VAT-free importation of capital equipment; investors sank 'hundreds of millions of dollars' building huge power plants; 'government reneged on its promise to exempt them from VAT'

BIR-refund procedural complaint verbatim from JFC: 'here is where the system fails: getting the VAT refunded is complicated and overly bureaucratic, with BIR forcing applicants to go to court, then causing delays in procedures in Court of Tax Appeals and up to Supreme Court... How can investors be encouraged to risk their money if they cannot rely on the solemn word of government?'

San Roque preview: example cited -- denied promised VAT refund of about P500 million 'because of alleged midstream change of rules that were retroactively applied. I will write on the details of this case at another time' (delivered in A457 June 9)

'Centavo-wise and peso-foolish' policy-critique close: 'past regimes have resorted to legalistic contortions to avoid honoring commitments. Now is the time to right this wrong... refrain from using technicalities to avoid them. Let us stop the insidious practice of being centavo-wise and peso-foolish'

'Proclamations by projection' second-half coda -- follow-up to A458 last Sunday; Brillantes said Comelec 'used projections from so-called grouped canvass reports in proclaiming top senatorial winners'; CJP: 'I do not wish to embarrass Brillantes further' but election law requires 'only official certificates of canvass (COC), not any other documents or inventions'; Comelec 'has absolutely no power to amend, much less to supersede, this law by passing a self-serving resolution authorizing itself to use mere projections from guesstimates'; 'wayward proclamations should not stay a minute longer in our legal firmament, lest they be used as mischievous precedents... in 2016 presidential election'; 'damned in history for inventing these bizarre proclamations by projection'
sub_topics: Now that President Aquino has thumbed down proposals to change economic provisions of our Constitution
Our officials should turn to other ways of attracting long-term foreign direct investments (FDIs)
These are kind of investments that spur inclusive growth, alleviate poverty and create jobs
Unfortunately, FDIs have, in past, come in trickles although they have been poured massively on our neighboring countries like Malaysia, Thailand, Singapore and Indonesia
Why? Because, CJP believes, most important incentive to bring them in -- trustworthiness of our government -- has been neglected
Past regimes are not famous for honoring their word
In contrast, can present administration be trusted?
Is it sensitive and responsive to investors' cry for fairness, honesty and transparency?
Testing P-Noy administration's trustworthiness is recent letter of Joint Foreign Chambers (JFC) lamenting failure of government to fulfill its commitments
This lament cannot be ignored because JFC represents largest existing FDIs in Philippines
For uninitiated, let CJP explain that large foreign investors have wide options on where to invest their billions
Their choices naturally depend on how safe their money would be, how easy or how difficult it is to do business in country
And how much they would earn for risks they take
To lure large FDIs, countries compete by showing their advantages as desirable business venues with reasonable rates of return
They offer various incentives, which always include tax- and duty-free importation of capital equipment that investors need to bring into country
To understand this competition, let us look at parallel in consumer trade
People choose and buy cars of specific brand because they trust its engineering, beauty, after-sale service and used-car prices
In same manner, investors choose countries that offer real and believable value for their money
To attract FDIs to solve power outages in 1990s, our government promised many fiscal incentives and benefits
Including VAT-free importation of capital equipment
Naturally, in making business plans, investors included these fiscal incentives in computing their risks and possible earnings
And compared them with those offered by other countries
In its pained letter to Finance Secretary Cesar Purisima, JFC wrote that after its members sank in hundreds of millions of dollars in building huge power plants
Government reneged on its promise to exempt them from VAT (value-added taxes)
Procedurally, investors were first required to pay VAT, and then to apply for refund from Bureau of Internal Revenue
According to JFC, 'here is where system fails: getting VAT refunded is complicated and overly bureaucratic'
'With BIR forcing applicants to go to court, then causing delays in procedures in Court of Tax Appeals and up to Supreme Court'
'How can investors be encouraged to risk their money if they cannot rely on solemn word of government?'
As example of how our government has over past many years reneged on its commitments
JFC cited case of San Roque Power Corp.
Which -- after over decade of grueling litigation -- was denied its promised VAT refund of about P500 million
Because of alleged midstream change of rules that were retroactively applied
CJP will write on details of this case at another time (A457)
CJP's point now is this: government must honor its commitments promptly
For too long, past regimes have resorted to legalistic contortions to avoid honoring commitments
Now is time to right this wrong
To attract long-term FDIs that spur inclusive growth, alleviate poverty, and create jobs
Present administration must show investors that it will honor commitments made by our country
And will refrain from using technicalities to avoid them
Let us stop insidious practice of being centavo-wise and peso-foolish
Proclamations by projection: in response to CJP's column last Sunday (A458)
Comelec Chair Sixto Brillantes Jr. said that poll body used projections from so-called 'grouped canvass reports' in proclaiming top senatorial winners
CJP does not wish to embarrass Brillantes further by stressing that our election law requires use only of official certificates of canvass (COC)
Not any other documents or inventions, to proclaim winners

And that Comelec has absolutely no power to amend, much less to supersede, this law by passing self-serving resolution authorizing itself to use mere projections from 'guesstimates' extrapolated from these grouped canvass reports
However, these baseless proclamations by projection must be corrected and banished from our election lingo
Preferably by Comelec itself, by withdrawing them and reproclaiming senatorial winners with use of completed COCs
Poll body should not wait for Supreme Court or Congress to reverse and censure it
Yes, these wayward proclamations should not stay minute longer in our legal firmament
Lest they be used as mischievous precedents to proclaim alleged winners in 2016 presidential election
Comelec would be well advised to correct this mischief now
Otherwise, instead of being hailed for what it trumpets as generally successful automated election
Present Comelec will be damned in history for inventing these bizarre proclamations by projection

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban writes the third installment of his automated-elections quadrilogy -- one week after A458 -- and uses the first half to launch his most-important-investment-incentive thesis (trustworthiness), which Sunday A457 will follow up with the full San Roque Power case-study; the second half delivers the 'Proclamations by projection' coda. Now that President Aquino has thumbed down proposals to change the economic provisions of our Constitution, our officials should turn to other ways of attracting long-term FDIs -- these are the kind of investments that spur inclusive growth, alleviate poverty and create jobs; unfortunately, FDIs have, in the past, come in trickles although they have been poured massively on our neighboring countries like Malaysia, Thailand, Singapore and Indonesia. Trustworthiness: why? because, CJ believes, the most important incentive to bring them in -- the trustworthiness of our government -- has been neglected; past regimes are not famous for honoring their word; in contrast, can the present administration be trusted? Is it sensitive and responsive to investors' cry for fairness, honesty and transparency? Testing the PNoy administration's trustworthiness is a recent letter of the JFC lamenting the failure of the government to fulfill its commitments -- this lament cannot be ignored because the JFC represents the largest existing FDIs in the Philippines. For the uninitiated, let CJ explain that large foreign investors have wide options on where to invest their billions; their choices naturally depend on how safe their money would be, how easy or how difficult it is to do business in the country, and how much they would earn for the risks they take; to lure large FDIs, countries compete by showing their advantages as desirable business venues with reasonable rates of return -- they offer various incentives, which always include tax- and duty-free importation of capital equipment that investors need to bring into the country; to understand this competition, let us look at a parallel in the consumer trade -- people choose and buy cars of a specific brand because they trust its engineering, beauty, after-sale service and used-car prices; in the same manner, investors choose countries that offer real and believable value for their money. Pained letter: to attract FDIs to solve the power outages in the 1990s, our government promised many fiscal incentives and benefits, including VAT-free importation of capital equipment; naturally, in making business plans, investors included these fiscal incentives in computing their risks and possible earnings, and compared them with those offered by other countries; in its pained letter to Finance Sec. Cesar Purisima, the JFC wrote that after its members sank in hundreds of millions of dollars in building huge power plants, the government reneged on its promise to exempt them from VAT; procedurally, investors were first required to pay the VAT, and then to apply for refund from the BIR. According to the JFC, 'here is where the system fails: getting the VAT refunded is complicated and overly bureaucratic, with the BIR forcing applicants to go to court, then causing delays in procedures in the Court of Tax Appeals and up to the Supreme Court... How can investors be encouraged to risk their money if they cannot rely on the solemn word of government?' As an example of how our government has over the past many years reneged on its commitments, the JFC cited the case of San Roque Power Corp., which -- after over a decade of grueling litigation -- was denied its promised VAT refund of about P500 million because of alleged midstream change of rules that were retroactively applied; CJ will write on the details of this case at another time (A457). CJ's point now is this: the government must honor its commitments promptly -- for too long, past regimes have resorted to legalistic contortions to avoid honoring commitments; now is the time to right this wrong; to attract long-term FDIs that spur inclusive growth, alleviate poverty, and create jobs, the present administration must show investors that it will honor commitments made by our country, and will refrain from using technicalities to avoid them; let us stop the insidious practice of being centavo-wise and peso-foolish. Proclamations by projection: in response to CJ's column last Sunday (A458), Comelec Chair Sixto Brillantes Jr. said that the poll body used projections from so-called 'grouped canvass reports' in proclaiming the top senatorial winners; CJ does not wish to embarrass Brillantes further by stressing that our election law requires the use only of official COCs, not any other documents or inventions, to proclaim winners -- and that the Comelec has absolutely no power to amend, much less to supersede, this law by passing a self-serving resolution authorizing itself to use mere projections from 'guesstimates' extrapolated from these grouped canvass reports. However, these baseless proclamations by projection must be corrected and banished from our election lingo, preferably by the Comelec itself, by withdrawing them and reproclaiming the senatorial winners with the use of the completed COCs; the poll body should not wait for the SC or Congress to reverse and censure it -- yes, these wayward proclamations should not stay a minute longer in our legal firmament, lest they be used as mischievous precedents to proclaim the alleged winners in the 2016 presidential election; the Comelec would be well advised to correct this mischief now -- otherwise, instead of being hailed for what it trumpets as a generally successful automated election, the present Comelec will be damned in history for inventing these bizarre proclamations by projection.
